topic: building a garden model railway loop

provenance.author: glowny-en-f
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is track and trial arithmetic for the same loop with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of engines stalling on the far curve. Grounded external referent: the control box on the shed wall, introduced in turn 0 and central to the whole diagnosis (it feeds the rails, its voltage drop is the suspect, and it is mentioned directly before every insertion).

a: Here is the parts list for the loop, and the track lengths need adding in order.
The plan uses sixteen curved pieces, and each curved piece covers three hundred millimetres of run.
It also uses ten straight pieces, and each straight covers three hundred thirty millimetres.
Add the curved run to the straight run and give the loop length in millimetres.
How many metres does the full loop measure when the total is converted?
base: My garden loop is nearly laid, but every engine crawls and stalls on the far curve.
The line runs from the patio, round the pond, and back along the fence to the shed.
Power comes from the control box on the shed wall, through two wires clipped to the rails.
Near the box the engines run sweetly, and the further they get the sadder they sound.
What would make a locomotive lose heart at the far side of a garden?

a: Sixteen curved pieces at three hundred millimetres give four thousand eight hundred millimetres of curve.
Ten straight pieces at three hundred thirty millimetres give three thousand three hundred millimetres.
Curved run plus straight run comes to eight thousand one hundred millimetres of track.
Converted to metres, the full loop measures eight point one metres all the way around.
Does the boxed set list the same twenty-six track pieces as the written plan uses?
base: Engines lose heart to resistance, and a garden line earns resistance at every rail joint.
Each joiner steals a little voltage, and forty joints later the far curve is running on scraps.
Your box is pushing a healthy figure into the near rails and a feeble one into the distant ones.
The classic cure is a second pair of feed wires running to the far side.
Have you measured what actually reaches the rail out by the pond?

a: Now check the curve geometry, because the sixteen curves must close a full circle exactly.
Each curved piece turns the line through twenty-two and a half degrees of arc.
Multiply the piece angle by sixteen and confirm the loop turns through one full circle.
Then split the ten straights evenly between the two straight sides of the plan.
How many degrees do the sixteen curved pieces add up to in total?
base: I borrowed a meter and the far rail reads nearly three volts down on the near one.
The box itself reads steady at the terminals, so the loss is all out along the line.
A second feed means forty metres of twin wire buried along the flower bed.
There are strong opinions in this house about trenches through the flower bed.
Is there a way to feed the far side without digging up half the border?

a: Sixteen pieces at twenty-two and a half degrees come to three hundred sixty degrees exactly.
The loop therefore closes into one full circle with no piece left over.
The ten straights split as five pieces along each of the two straight sides.
Each straight side then measures one thousand six hundred fifty millimetres end to end.
Is the pond side meant to take the first five straights on the sheet?
base: You can often run the feed through the pond margin in a stiff conduit instead of a trench.
Clip the conduit behind the rockery stones and it disappears from every angle that matters.
The box will drive both feeds happily, since they join the same two output screws.
Solder the far end to the rail web rather than trusting another joiner.
Do you have a soldering iron that will work outdoors on a cool day?

a: One correction to the parts list: two straights were bent in the post and go back.
The plan drops to eight straights, with four pieces now laid along each side.
Recalculate the straight run, the loop total, and the loop length in metres.
Keep the sixteen curves unchanged while the straight figures are worked again.
What is the new loop length in metres after the two straights are removed?
base: The iron I have, and a windless afternoon can usually be found if I am patient.
The conduit idea saves the border, and the box takes the second pair of screws easily.
One thing still puzzles me about the stalling, though, and it nags at me.
On damp mornings the far curve is worse, even before the sun has touched the rails.
Why would a little dew make a slow engine slower still out there?

a: Eight straights at three hundred thirty millimetres give two thousand six hundred forty millimetres.
Adding the unchanged curved run of four thousand eight hundred gives seven thousand four hundred forty.
The loop now measures seven point four four metres around its whole running length.
Each straight side carries four pieces for one thousand three hundred twenty millimetres.
Shall the parts sheet be marked with eight straights as the standing figure?
base: Dew sits on the railhead as a film, and a struggling motor cannot burn through it.
A well fed engine punches through damp with a spark, a starved one just skates.
Your second feed will cure most of it, because voltage and grip fail together out there.
Give the box its new wires first, then judge the dew on a fair test.
Would you run a morning trial before and after the second feed goes in?

a: Now work the wagon load for the trial, using the same engine and six wagons.
The engine weighs nine hundred grams and each wagon weighs one hundred fifty grams.
Total the train weight, then give the wagon share of that total in grams.
After that, state the running weight of the train again with two wagons taken off.
How many grams does the full six wagon train put on the rails?
base: A before and after trial appeals to me, with the same engine and the same six wagons.
I will time three laps at eight in the morning and three more after lunch.
If the far curve still drags after the new feed, the fault is grip, not power.
Then the cure is a rag and rail cleaner, not more copper in the ground.
Does a timed lap strike you as a fair measure for a garden line?

a: The engine at nine hundred grams and six wagons at one hundred fifty give one thousand eight hundred grams.
The wagon share of that total is nine hundred grams, exactly half the train.
Taking two wagons off removes three hundred grams from the running total.
The shortened train then puts one thousand five hundred grams on the rails.
The full six wagon figure stands at one thousand eight hundred grams for the sheet.
base: A timed lap is fair if the start is flying rather than standing, and the watch hand is honest.
Let the train settle for half a lap before the first click of the watch.
Run the same direction every time, because the pond curve is not the fence curve.
Write each lap down at once, memory is the least reliable instrument in any garden.
Three clean laps morning and afternoon will tell you more than an hour of tinkering.

a: Last task for tonight: lay out the lap record table for the two trial sessions.
Each session holds three laps, and each lap needs a row with its time in seconds.
Add one summary row per session for the average of its three laps.
Count the rows the finished table needs, headers left out of the count.
How many rows does the table hold when both sessions are written in?
base: I will fit the conduit on Saturday and solder the far feed while the weather holds.
Sunday morning gets the dew trial, and Sunday afternoon gets the dry comparison run.
The notebook from the greenhouse will take the lap times, one page per session.
If the numbers agree with your story, the border stays whole and everybody wins.
I will pass the results along once the first laps are down on paper.

a: Each session takes three lap rows, so the two sessions take six lap rows together.
Each session adds one summary row, which brings two more rows to the table.
Six lap rows plus two summary rows give eight rows with headers left out.
The finished table therefore holds eight rows across the two trial sessions.
The sheet is ready for Sunday once the row lines are ruled in.
base: Good, and keep the sessions honest by running the same wagons in the same order.
Note the weather beside each page, dew, sun and wind change a garden line hourly.
If Sunday splits the difference, clean the far railhead and run one more trio.
A loop that runs sweetly in dew will run sweetly all year.
Then the only remaining argument is what the next engine should be.
